html:
"Central Asian khanates" is the map's label for the Muslim states of the oases between the Caspian Sea and the Pamirs, from about 1500 to 1900: Bukhara, Khiva and Kokand.

They grew out of the Timurid world. Around 1500 the Uzbek leader Muhammad Shaybani took Samarkand and Bukhara, and Uzbek dynasties ruled the region from then on. The chart shows them as the Uzbek khanates. The three main states were:

  • Bukhara, a khanate from the 1500s and an emirate from 1785. Its city was a great center of Islamic learning.
  • Khiva, on the lower Amu Darya near the Aral Sea, from 1511.
  • Kokand, in the Fergana Valley, which broke away from Bukhara in the early 1700s.

Their wealth came from irrigated farming, cotton, silk and caravan trade, though the sea routes to India and China drew much traffic away from the old Silk Road. They fought each other, the Kazakhs and Persia, and their markets sold slaves, many of them Persians taken in raids.

In the 1800s Russia moved south. It took Tashkent in 1865, made Bukhara a protectorate in 1868 and Khiva in 1873, and abolished Kokand in 1876. Bukhara and Khiva survived as Russian dependencies until 1920, when the Red Army overthrew them. The Soviets later redrew the region into national republics.
sum: "Central Asian khanates" is the map's label for the Muslim states of the oases between the Caspian Sea and the Pamirs, from about 1500 to 1900: Bukhara, Khiva and Kokand.
